bonds.title: The station guide
bonds.busy: I'm meeting a group off the Shinkansen. Find me here in the daytime or the early evening, when the tower lights up.

ranks.title: The lighthouse
ranks.invite: You keep looking up at the tower. Everyone does. Have you a little of the {slot}? I'll tell you what it's supposed to be.
talk: Kyoto Tower is a lighthouse. That was the idea in 1964: a city with no sea, so a light over a sea of tiled roofs.
There's no steel skeleton inside. The skin is the structure, welded steel plate, like the shell of a prawn. 131 metres, standing on a nine-storey building.
ranks.fact: Kyoto Tower, opened in December 1964, is 131 m tall and has no steel frame: its welded steel skin carries the load.

ask.q: Guess what people said when it went up.

options.reply: Exactly that, and louder. There were petitions. Sixty years on, it's the first thing we look for from the train.
Not a bit. There were petitions against it. It took about a generation for it to mean home.

request.text: Stand at the foot of Kyoto Tower and look straight up
request.ask: Have you stood right under the tower yet? Across the road, at its foot. Look straight up, then come back.

ranks.title: A word at the rank
talk: Dizzy? Most visitors think it's twice the height it is, because nothing near it is tall.
The drivers on the rank by the Karasuma exit bring my groups back when their feet give out. I've told them you're one of mine.
ranks.fact: Kyoto Tower's observation deck is 100 m above the street; the tower stands on a nine-storey building opposite the station's Karasuma exit.

gives.name: A word at the rank
gives.text: 30% off every taxi in central Kyoto

request.text: Take a taxi somewhere (a hand up at the kerb, Y)
request.ask: Have you used the rank yet? A hand up at the kerb. Tell the driver Haruka sent you.

ranks.title: Up and down
talk: You'll have noticed the driver didn't want an address. He wanted a crossing.
The streets still follow the grid laid out in 794, and we give directions by it. North is 'up', agaru; south is 'down', sagaru. Karasuma-Shijo agaru: from that crossing, go north.
ranks.fact: Central Kyoto keeps the grid of the capital laid out in 794, and addresses still say agaru (go north) or sagaru (go south) from a named crossing.

ask.q: So 'Karasuma-Shijo sagaru' is which way from the crossing?

options.reply: Yes. And down really is down: the station sits some twenty metres lower than the Palace gardens.
The other way. Up is north, where the Palace is, and the land rises towards it: some twenty metres from here.

request.text: Go up the grid to the Imperial Gardens
request.ask: Go up to the Imperial Gardens once. Walk it if you can: you'll feel the slope in your calves.

ranks.title: The great stairs
talk: You went up. Now you know what 'up' means here.
The station was the next fight after the tower. Hara Hiroshi's building, 1997: 470 metres long, and people called it a wall across the city.
Climb the great stairs inside it some evening. A hundred and seventy-one steps, and nobody arguing at the top.
ranks.fact: Kyoto Station Building, designed by Hara Hiroshi and opened in 1997, is 470 m long; its Grand Staircase has 171 steps.

gives.name: Haruka's introduction
gives.text: 15% more for every job in central Kyoto

request.text: Take one photograph at golden or blue hour (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Bring me one picture in the low light, when the tower goes orange. Photo mode, then come back.

ranks.title: Home
talk: That's the hour. All day the tower is white and nobody looks; then the sun goes and it's a candle, whatever the architect said.
I told you people hated it. My grandmother did. Then she'd come back from Osaka, see it from the train window, and say 'ah, we're home.'
You'll do the same, next time. That's how you'll know.
ranks.fact: Kyoto Tower was designed by the architect Yamada Mamoru in the image of a lighthouse for a city without a sea.

gives.name: Up and down
gives.text: Bearings, from someone born on the grid

bonds.title: The monk at the gate
bonds.busy: Forgive me, I have duties in the hall. I am at the gate in the mornings, before the tour buses.

ranks.title: Before the buses
ranks.invite: You are early. That is rare, and welcome. Might you have a little of the {slot}? The hall is at its best before the buses.
talk: The gates open before six in summer, and the morning service begins at seven, every day of the year. Anyone may sit at the back. Most of Kyoto does not know this.
The Founder's Hall is seventy-six metres across and thirty-eight high. Nine hundred and twenty-seven tatami. I have counted them while sweeping, though not on purpose.
ranks.fact: Higashi Honganji's Founder's Hall, rebuilt in 1895, is 76 m wide, 58 m deep and 38 m high, with 927 tatami mats inside.

ask.q: Why would one build a hall so large, do you think?

options.reply: Just so. Farmers and townspeople paid for it, and it was built so that all of them could come in at once. It is a room, not a monument.
The neighbours were impressed, I am told. But ordinary followers built it, so that all of them might fit inside at once.

request.text: Walk west to Nishi Hongwanji, the other half
request.ask: Have you walked west to the other Honganji yet? Ten minutes. It is older than we are, and does not let us forget.

ranks.title: East and West
talk: So you have seen our elder brother. We were one temple until 1602, when Tokugawa Ieyasu gave this land to a second line of abbots. Two are easier to govern than one.
We have burned four times since. The last was in 1864, in the fighting at the Palace gates. What stands now was finished in 1895.
Which reminds me. The hall wants incense, and the shop is over by our brother's gate. It is a paid errand, if you would.
ranks.fact: Higashi Honganji was founded in 1602 on land given by Tokugawa Ieyasu, dividing the Honganji in two; it burned four times in the Edo period, the last in 1864.

gives.name: The temple's errand
gives.text: A paid errand for the hall, in your diary under Work

request.text: Fetch the incense for the Founder's Hall
request.ask: The incense is waiting at the shop by Nishi Hongwanji. It is in your diary, under Work.

ranks.title: The hair ropes
talk: Thank you. The hall smells of itself again.
When these halls were raised, no rope would hold the great timbers. So women across the country cut their hair and sent it, and it was twisted with hemp into ropes.
Fifty-three were made. One is kept in a glass case in the corridor. Children are frightened of it, and adults go quiet.
ranks.fact: The ropes that hauled Higashi Honganji's timbers were twisted from followers' hair and hemp: 53 were made, the largest 110 m long and about a tonne.

options.text: Yes, if it was all I had
options.reply: That is what they wrote, in the letters that came with it. 'It is all I have.' Thank you.
Many did so. The hair came from those who had none to send.

request.text: Eat something at a counter in the city
request.ask: Have you eaten? One should not listen to an old monk on an empty stomach. Nishiki is a walk north of here.

ranks.title: The moat
talk: You look fed. Good.
Look down as you leave: there is a moat along Karasuma-dori, with carp in it. A temple with a moat. We were given this land by a shogun, and it shows.
The water came by its own pipe from the Lake Biwa Canal, laid in 1897 for fighting fires. After four fires one takes precautions.
ranks.fact: The Honganji Waterworks, a dedicated pipe from the Lake Biwa Canal at Keage, was laid in 1897 to protect Higashi Honganji from fire; it fed the moat along Karasuma-dori.

gives.name: Known at the temple
gives.text: 10% more for every job in central Kyoto

request.text: Come to Higashi Honganji for the morning service
request.ask: Come one morning at seven and sit at the back. You need not understand a word.

ranks.title: The back row
talk: You came, and you sat, and you did not take a photograph. I noticed.
People ask what we chant. It is one name, said by a great many people over seven hundred years. That is all the hall is for.
The gate opens before six. You know where the back row is.
ranks.fact: Higashi Honganji is the head temple of the Otani branch of Jodo Shinshu, the school founded on the teaching of Shinran (1173-1263).

gives.name: Before the buses
gives.text: Light: you know the first hour of the day

bonds.title: The pickle stall
bonds.busy: I'm selling, dear, or I'm shut. Come in market hours, morning and through the day. We're all gone by six.

ranks.title: Cold wells
ranks.invite: You're looking, not buying. That's all right. Have you a bit of the {slot}? I'll show you the market properly.
talk: Nishiki is three hundred and ninety metres end to end, about a hundred and thirty shops. Look up: the roof is red, yellow and green glass, so you always know where you are.
It started with fish. There's cold water under this street, good wells, and before ice that was everything. The fishmongers got their licence in 1615.
ranks.fact: Nishiki Market runs 390 m between Takakura and Teramachi streets with about 130 shops; its fish market was officially licensed in 1615.

ask.q: Why do you think a fish market grew up this far from the sea?

options.reply: Listen to you. Yes: the wells kept the fish, and the Palace was a short walk north to buy it.
Too far off, dear. It was the wells: cold water, right under our feet.

request.ask: Have you tasted anything yet? You can't know a market with your eyes.

ranks.title: An errand
talk: Good. You eat like you mean it.
Mr. Tanaka from Tokyo orders pickles for his meetings and never has time to fetch them. You've got legs. It pays, and he tips when he's embarrassed.
ranks.fact: Kyoto's three classic pickles are senmaizuke (sliced turnip), suguki (fermented turnip) and shibazuke (aubergine with red shiso).

gives.name: Mrs. Nakamura's runner
gives.text: A paid delivery from the stall, in your diary under Work

request.ask: The box is tied and waiting. It's in your diary, under Work.

ranks.title: A thousand slices
talk: He rang to say thank you. He never rings.
Now, senmaizuke. Shogoin turnip, big as your head, sliced so thin you could read through it, laid down with kombu. A cook from the Palace kitchens came up with it in 1865.
We only make it in the cold months. If someone sells it to you in August, smile and keep walking.
ranks.fact: Senmaizuke, thin-sliced Shogoin turnip pickled with kombu, was devised in 1865 by Daito Tozaburo, a former cook at the Imperial Palace, and is made from late autumn to early spring.

ask.q: So when would you come back for it?

options.reply: You were listening. Come in December; I'll keep you the middle of the barrel.
I just told you, dear. Cold months. Turnips don't care what visitors want.

request.ask: Eat your way along a bit further first. When you can tell dashi from sugar, come back.

ranks.title: The greengrocer's son
talk: Now you've a tongue. So I'll tell you about our painter.
Ito Jakuchu. Born here in 1716, eldest son of Masuya, a greengrocers' wholesale house at the Takakura end. He ran the shop till he was forty, then gave it to his brother and painted chickens.
There's a shrine at the far end of the street, Nishiki Tenmangu. Go and look hard at its torii, then tell me what's wrong with it.
ranks.fact: The painter Ito Jakuchu was born in 1716 as heir to Masuya, a greengrocers' wholesaler in Nishiki Market, and gave up the business at forty to paint.

gives.name: Market rate
gives.text: 20% more for every job in central Kyoto

request.text: Walk to the east end of Nishiki: the torii of Nishiki Tenmangu
request.ask: Have you been to the Teramachi end yet? Look up at the shrine's torii. Properly.

ranks.title: The torii in the wall
talk: You saw it. The ends of the torii go straight into the buildings either side. The gate was there first; the shops grew up round it, and nobody was going to cut a torii.
That's this street. Nothing gets knocked down. It gets built around. Four hundred years of it.
Come in the cold and I'll have your turnip. Middle of the barrel. I don't say that to visitors.
ranks.fact: At Nishiki Tenmangu, the shrine at the market's east end, the tips of the stone torii's lintel run into the buildings on either side.

gives.name: The middle of the barrel
gives.text: Taste, from someone who salts it herself

bonds.title: The castle guide
bonds.busy: I've a group at the gate. Catch me in the daytime, while the castle's open: we shut at five.

ranks.title: The singing floor
ranks.invite: You stopped to listen. Good sign. Have you some of the {slot}? I'll tell you the story, and then the true one.
talk: The story: the floors of the Ninomaru Palace sing so that no assassin could cross them. I tell it six times a day and people love it.
The true one: it's the iron clamps under the boards, rubbing on their nails as the wood moves. Nobody designed it. The castle's own notice says so, in small print.
ranks.fact: The 'nightingale floors' of Nijo Castle's Ninomaru Palace squeak because the iron clamps under the boards rub against their nails, not by design.

ask.q: Which one should I tell tomorrow's group?

options.reply: That's what I do. Story first, truth second. They remember both.
Then they'd fall asleep. Story first, then the truth: that way they keep both.

request.text: Photograph Nijo Castle's walls and moat (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Take me a picture of the walls over the moat. Photo mode. I collect other people's.

ranks.title: The corner turret
talk: Nice. The turret on the south-east corner is one of two left. There were four; the others went in the great fire of 1788.
So did the palace of the inner ward. And the keep had already gone: struck by lightning in 1750 and never rebuilt. People walk right over where it stood, looking for it.
ranks.fact: Nijo Castle's five-storey keep was destroyed by lightning in 1750 and never rebuilt; the great fire of 1788 took the inner palace and two of the four corner turrets.

gives.name: A guide's eye
gives.text: Eye: you judge a wall at a glance

request.text: Guess a building's height to within a quarter (G)
request.ask: Try your eye: pick the turret or the gate, press G, and tell me how close you came.

ranks.title: 1603 and 1867
talk: You've got the eye. So, the two dates that matter.
1603: Ieyasu builds this place to show that the Tokugawa run the country. 1867: the last shogun, Yoshinobu, calls his lords into the great hall here and gives the country back.
Same family, same palace, two hundred and sixty-four years apart. I never get tired of saying it.
ranks.fact: Tokugawa Ieyasu had Nijo Castle built in 1603; in October 1867 the last shogun, Yoshinobu, announced the return of power to the emperor in its Ninomaru Palace.

ask.q: And how often did the shoguns come, in between?

options.reply: Right. From 1634 to 1863 not one shogun set foot in it. Two hundred and twenty-nine years of very careful dusting.
You'd think so. From 1634 to 1863, not once. Two hundred and twenty-nine years of dusting.

request.text: Answer the visitors at the castle gate
request.ask: People at the gate keep asking me the way. Stand in for me once: it's in your diary, under Work.

ranks.title: The palace that moved
talk: They say you pointed straight. I'd expect nothing less.
The palace in the inner ward isn't from here. It was a prince's house beside the Imperial Palace, the Katsura family's, taken apart and carried over in 1893.
It was shut for eighteen years and opened again in September 2024. I walked the first group through. Best day of the job.
ranks.fact: Nijo Castle's Honmaru Palace is the former Katsura-no-miya residence, moved from beside the Imperial Palace in 1893-94; it reopened in September 2024 after about 18 years closed.

gives.name: A guide's commission
gives.text: 15% more for every job in central Kyoto

request.ask: Keep guessing heights. When you can call the gate to the metre, come and find me.

ranks.title: Fifty kinds of cherry
talk: To the metre. You could do my job, and I'd like it noted that I said so first.
Last thing. Come back in spring: about three hundred cherry trees in here, fifty kinds, so something is in flower from mid-March to late April.
They light them at night. I work those evenings for nothing. Don't tell the office.
ranks.fact: Nijo Castle has about 300 cherry trees of some 50 varieties, flowering in turn from mid-March to late April.

gives.name: To the metre
gives.text: Eye, from a man who measures gates

jobs.title: Which way from the castle?
jobs.blurb: Visitors at Nijo's east gate ask the way. Face each place's true bearing; the nearer, the better the pay.
jobs.who: A couple with a paper map
jobs.done: They bow, and set off the right way.

jobs.title: The tower and the temple
jobs.blurb: A travel page wants Kyoto Tower, the station's front and Higashi Honganji's great hall. Photo mode (O); golden or blue hour pays a quarter more.
jobs.done: The editor writes back: 'The low light suits it.'

jobs.title: A fare to Nijo Castle
jobs.blurb: Drive your own car as a cab: pick up at the station's Karasuma kerb and take your passengers up to Nijo Castle's east gate.
jobs.to_name: Nijo Castle's east gate, on Horikawa-dori
jobs.text: "Nijo-jo, please. Horikawa-dori agaru, the east gate. We've a ticket for eleven."

jobs.title: Pickles for a meeting
jobs.blurb: From Mrs. Nakamura's stall in Nishiki to Mr. Tanaka, in the office streets by Karasuma-Shijo, before his meeting starts.
jobs.text: One cedar box of shibazuke and suguki, tied with string. Keep it level.
jobs.done: Mr. Tanaka bows too many times.

jobs.title: Incense for the Founder's Hall
jobs.blurb: From the incense shop by Nishi Hongwanji's gate across to Brother Sozen at Higashi Honganji.
jobs.at_name: the incense shop by Nishi Hongwanji
jobs.text: A paper parcel of sandalwood sticks. It scents your sleeve the whole way.
jobs.done: Brother Sozen receives it with both hands.

shops.name: Dashimaki counter だし巻き
shops.hello: Hai, irasshai! Just rolled, still hot.

menu.name: Dashimaki on a stick
menu.text: A rolled omelette that is nearly half stock: kombu and bonito, no sugar. It weeps when you bite it. Kyoto makes it savoury; Tokyo's is sweet.

menu.name: Tako tamago
menu.text: A baby octopus glazed dark red on a skewer, with a quail's egg tucked into its head. Nishiki's best-known mouthful.

shops.name: Mrs. Nakamura's pickles 漬物
shops.hello: Tsukemono, fresh today! Taste first, dear, then decide.

menu.name: Shibazuke
menu.text: Aubergine and cucumber salted down with red shiso until the whole barrel turns purple. Sour, sharp, and from Ohara, in the hills north of the city.

menu.name: Suguki
menu.text: A turnip from the Kamigamo fields, fermented under a weighted lever with nothing but salt. Sour like good yoghurt. Kyoto's winter pickle.

shops.name: Station kiosk 京みやげ
shops.hello: Welcome. Something for the train, or something to take home?

menu.name: Nama yatsuhashi
menu.text: Soft triangles of rice dough scented with cinnamon, folded over red bean. The baked kind came first: a hard biscuit curved like a koto.

menu.name: A folding fan 京扇子
menu.text: Bamboo ribs and paper, made in Kyoto in more than eighty steps, passed from one craftsman to the next. It opens with one hand, once you know how.

events.title: Gion Matsuri: the eve
events.text: The three evenings before the procession. The floats stand in the streets round Shijo-Karasuma, hung with lanterns, with musicians playing on them.
lines: The floats stand in the middle of the streets, each under a pyramid of paper lanterns. From the upper decks comes the music, flutes and bells: kon-chiki-chin, over and over.
Twenty-three floats take part in the first procession. On the last two evenings Shijo and Karasuma are closed to cars, and the whole district walks.

events.title: Gion Matsuri: the float procession
events.text: At 9:00 the Naginata-hoko leads the floats east from Shijo-Karasuma. A second, smaller procession follows on 24 July.
lines: Nine o'clock. The Naginata-hoko moves off first, as it does every year, with a boy in white make-up on its deck and a halberd on top, some twenty-five metres up.
The great floats weigh around ten tonnes and cannot steer. At each corner the pullers lay wet bamboo under the wheels and drag them round a heave at a time, to applause.

events.title: Aoi Matsuri
events.verb: Watch the procession leave the Palace
events.text: On 15 May at 10:30, about five hundred people in Heian court dress leave the Imperial Palace for the two Kamo shrines. Put off a day when it rains.
lines: Half past ten. Out of the Palace gate come riders, ox-carts hung with wisteria, and a lady in twelve layers of silk carried in a litter. About five hundred people, in the dress of a thousand years ago.
Everything wears heart-shaped hollyhock leaves: hats, carts, oxen. That is the aoi. The procession goes eight kilometres, to Shimogamo Shrine and then Kamigamo.

events.title: Jidai Matsuri
events.text: On 22 October at noon, about two thousand people in the dress of every age of the old capital walk from the Imperial Palace to Heian Jingu.
lines: Noon. A fife-and-drum band of 1868 comes first, and then the procession runs backwards through time: Edo, the warlords, the shoguns, all the way to the court of 794.
About two thousand people, two kilometres long. It began in 1895, the year Heian Jingu was built for the capital's eleven hundredth birthday. 22 October is the day the capital moved here.

events.title: Nijo Castle's cherries by night
events.verb: Join the queue for the lit cherries
events.text: From mid-March to mid-April in most years the castle opens again after dark, from 18:00 to 22:00, with its cherries lit.
lines: The queue runs along the moat. Inside, about three hundred cherries of fifty kinds are lit from below, so that something is in flower all month.
The east gate's ironwork throws long shadows on the gravel, and nobody speaks above a murmur. In 2026 the evenings ran from 19 March to 19 April.
